neurips-2018-learning-from-discriminativ.tldr: Simple feature explanations can support efficient online classification with bounded mistakes.
paragraphs: A classifier can learn from more than a label: a teacher may also explain which feature distinguishes the correct category from an incorrect one. This paper formalizes such explanations as discriminative features and studies how to use them in an online multiclass learning process.

The authors show that the required explanations are available when the target is a decision tree or belongs to a specified subclass of disjunctive normal form formulas. They develop an efficient online algorithm that learns from this combination of labels and feature feedback.

The theoretical mistake bounds are tight and depend on the size of the target concept, rather than the total number of available features, which may even be infinite. Experiments demonstrate the procedure. The guarantee relies on the specified target classes and feedback model; it does not assert that arbitrary natural-language explanations automatically have these properties.

neurips-2018-mixture-matrix-completion-3.tldr: Mixture matrix completion allows individual observed entries to come from different low-rank matrices.
paragraphs: Matrix completion usually assumes that missing entries belong to one low-rank matrix. A broader model allows different columns to belong to different low-rank components. This paper goes further: in mixture matrix completion, the component assignment may vary separately for every entry.

This formulation offers additional flexibility for recommendation, completion, and clustering problems. The authors establish that the problem can be well posed, characterize precise information-theoretic identifiability conditions, and derive sample complexity. These questions determine whether the hidden components can be distinguished from the available observations at all.

They also present a practical algorithm and test it on synthetic and real data. Its performance is comparable to state-of-the-art methods for simpler related problems. The abstract does not provide numerical results or spell out the identifiability assumptions, so the theoretical claims should not be read as unconditional recovery from arbitrary incomplete mixtures.

neurips-2018-predictive-uncertainty-esti.tldr: Prior Networks distinguish uncertainty in the data from uncertainty caused by distributional mismatch.
paragraphs: A prediction can be uncertain because the data are inherently ambiguous, the model parameters are uncertain, or the input differs from the training distribution. These sources can call for different responses. This paper introduces Prior Networks to explicitly represent the distributional-mismatch component instead of absorbing it into other uncertainty measures.

A Prior Network parameterizes a prior distribution over predictive distributions. The paper focuses on classification and evaluates whether this representation can identify out-of-distribution inputs and detect classification mistakes. The experiments include synthetic data, MNIST, and CIFAR-10.

On MNIST and CIFAR-10, Prior Networks outperform previous methods on the reported detection tasks. The experiments also show a distinction between data uncertainty and distributional uncertainty that earlier non-Bayesian methods did not achieve. The abstract gives no detection rates, so the result establishes comparative evidence in these settings rather than a quantified guarantee of reliable uncertainty estimates everywhere.

neurips-2018-streamlining-variational-in.tldr: Streamlining constraints improve satisfiability search without committing immediately to individual variable values.
paragraphs: Survey propagation estimates how frequently variables take particular values among satisfying assignments. Solvers use these estimates to guide search, but the approximate marginals can contradict one another. Hard decisions based on them may therefore commit the search to an unhelpful branch.

The authors propose a more general branching strategy using streamlining constraints. These constraints avoid immediately fixing individual variables, providing another way to incorporate approximate inference into a constraint-satisfaction solver. The comparison is with decimation-based methods that make hard assignments.

On random k-SAT instances across several problem sizes, streamlined solvers consistently outperform the decimation-based alternatives. For k equal to 3, 4, 5, and 6, the average reduction in the gap between empirical performance and theoretical satisfiability limits is 16.3%. This figure describes that gap, not a universal runtime reduction or an improvement on every family of constraint-satisfaction problems.

neurips-2018-unsupervised-depth-estimati.tldr: DepthNets infer facial depth and transformations without ground-truth depth supervision.
paragraphs: This paper learns three-dimensional facial structure from a single image while also predicting how to transform a face toward a desired pose and geometry. Its supervision avoids ground-truth depth information, addressing a setting where collecting explicit three-dimensional labels would be difficult.

DepthNets infer depths for facial keypoints and use them as intermediate quantities in a differentiable loss. That loss supports predicting a three-dimensional affine transformation that maps inferred input keypoints onto the target’s two-dimensional keypoints. The learned depths therefore serve a concrete geometric matching objective.

The resulting system produces plausible transformations for frontalization, three-dimensional modeling, and warping toward another pose or facial geometry. The authors explicitly identify shortcomings in the formulation and explore adversarial image translation as post-processing to resynthesize complete head images. The abstract claims plausible transformations rather than verified recovery of each face’s true physical depth.

neurips-2019-a-stochastic-composite-grad.tldr: Incremental variance reduction extends efficient stochastic optimization to smooth composite objectives.
paragraphs: The paper studies an objective formed by applying a smooth, possibly nonconvex function to another smooth vector-valued mapping. The inner mapping is an expectation or a finite sum. This nesting makes stochastic gradients more complicated than those of an ordinary expected-value objective.

The proposed stochastic composite-gradient method incrementally reduces variance in estimates of both the inner mapping and its Jacobian. The outer composition still makes the resulting composite-gradient estimator biased, so the analysis must account for more than ordinary sampling variance.

The authors show complexity orders matching the best known first-order methods for corresponding expected-value and finite-sum nonconvex optimization problems, despite that additional composition. The contribution is a theoretical extension of efficient variance-reduction methods to a broader objective class. The abstract does not provide experimental benchmarks or the detailed smoothness constants, and its guarantees apply to the stated smooth composite setting.

neurips-2019-adaptive-temporal-differenc.tldr: State-specific confidence intervals guide a switch between temporal-difference and Monte Carlo evaluation.
paragraphs: Policy evaluation estimates the value of following a policy from observed trajectories. Temporal-difference learning and Monte Carlo evaluation have complementary bias-variance behavior: temporal-difference estimates often reduce variance but can introduce more bias. This paper studies on-policy value approximation from a fixed batch of trajectory data.

The authors argue that local approximation errors can be amplified through temporal-difference updates. Their algorithm learns confidence intervals that detect biased temporal-difference estimates and adaptively chooses between temporal-difference and Monte Carlo returns at each state, limiting the propagation of those errors.

Across several policy-evaluation tasks, this adaptive procedure is competitive with the best approach chosen afterward with hindsight. The evidence supports using estimated uncertainty to make local evaluation choices, rather than selecting one return estimator globally. The abstract does not give numerical error reductions or claim that the confidence intervals eliminate all approximation bias.

neurips-2019-defending-against-neural-fa.tldr: Grover demonstrates both risks of generated news and the value of generator-based detection.
paragraphs: The paper investigates automatically generated disinformation by developing Grover, a controllable text generator that can produce an article from a headline. Human evaluators find its generated disinformation more trustworthy than the human-written disinformation used in the study, illustrating a potential misuse risk rather than validating the generated claims.

The authors then examine detection. With a moderate amount of training data, existing discriminators distinguish generated fake news from real human-written news with 73% accuracy. Grover used as a detector achieves 92% accuracy, outperforming those alternatives in this evaluation.

Further analysis links detectable artifacts to exposure bias and to sampling strategies intended to reduce it. The study argues that access to strong generators can support defensive research and discusses ethical issues around release. Detection of generated text is the evaluated task; these accuracy figures should not be interpreted as general fact-checking performance or proof that all false articles can be identified.

neurips-2019-invert-to-learn-to-invert-6.tldr: Invertible networks enable deep iterative MRI reconstruction without storing every layer’s activations.
paragraphs: Learned iterative solvers can reconstruct images from indirect measurements, but training memory usually grows with network depth. That limits how many iterative layers can be used, especially for three-dimensional data. This paper targets the memory constraint in learning-based inverse-problem solvers.

The proposed iterative inverse model uses invertible networks so that intermediate activations do not all have to be stored during training. The authors describe a constant-memory approach with respect to depth, allowing substantially deeper reconstruction models within the available memory.

In an MRI reconstruction application, they train 400-layer models on three-dimensional volumes. Experiments on a public dataset achieve state-of-the-art reconstruction performance. The abstract attributes the opportunity to greater model depth and expressiveness, but does not provide numerical image-quality results or a runtime comparison. The demonstrated benefit is specific to the evaluated reconstruction setting and memory-saving architecture.

neurips-2019-learning-based-low-rank-app.tldr: Learning sparse sketch matrices improves low-rank approximation while mixed sketches retain worst-case guarantees.
paragraphs: Fast low-rank approximation often compresses a matrix with a sparse random sketch before applying singular-value decomposition. This paper asks whether prior examples of input matrices can help choose a better sketch. The goal remains minimizing Frobenius-norm approximation error for a rank-k result.

The authors learn a sketch matrix with the same sparsity as the random alternative. They also investigate mixed sketches with some learned rows and some random rows, combining data-dependent improvements with retained worst-case guarantees. Across multiple dataset types, learned sketches reduce approximation loss, sometimes by up to an order of magnitude.

The theoretical analysis includes an approximation algorithm for empirical-loss minimization in the special case of a single sketch row, with a factor depending on training matrices’ stable rank. Generalization bounds address transfer beyond training examples. The special-case optimization result and mixed-sketch guarantees should be distinguished from unrestricted claims about every fully learned sketch.

neurips-2019-learning-by-abstraction-the.tldr: The Neural State Machine answers image questions by reasoning over an inferred semantic graph.
paragraphs: Visual reasoning requires combining what is in an image with the relationships described by a question. The Neural State Machine aims to combine neural perception with a structured reasoning process, moving both visual and linguistic information into representations based on semantic concepts.

The model first predicts a probabilistic graph representing the image’s semantics. It then reasons sequentially over that graph, traversing nodes to answer a question or derive an inference. The graph functions as an intermediate world model, intended to make the reasoning more transparent and modular.

Evaluation on VQA-CP and GQA achieves state-of-the-art results in the reported comparisons. Additional experiments examine novel concept combinations, changes in answer distributions, and unseen linguistic structures, showing strong generalization across those tests. The abstract does not give scores or establish complete reasoning reliability; it supports the usefulness of this structured representation for the evaluated visual-question-answering tasks.

neurips-2019-learning-hawkes-processes-f.tldr: Variational expectation-maximization improves Hawkes-process learning from short event sequences.
paragraphs: Multivariate Hawkes processes describe how events in different streams influence future events. Learning their interaction network is harder when only short observation sequences are available, because limited data make maximum-likelihood estimates prone to overfitting. Regularization is therefore especially important in this setting.

The paper develops an efficient variational expectation-maximization algorithm that can optimize an expanded collection of hyperparameters. This addresses the limited flexibility of regularizers controlled by a single shared hyperparameter. It also learns a posterior over model parameters, allowing parameter uncertainty to enter the estimation process.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods when observation sequences are short. The abstract does not state sequence lengths, dataset names, or numerical gains. Its contribution is a more flexible regularization and uncertainty framework for learning event interactions under data scarcity, rather than a claim that short records always identify the true underlying network.

neurips-2019-mining-gold-samples-for-con.tldr: A discriminator-derived density gap improves conditional-GAN training, sampling, and data selection.
paragraphs: Conditional GANs generate examples associated with specified classes, but their generated distribution may still differ from the data distribution. This paper introduces the gap of log-densities, or GOLD, as a way to assess that mismatch on particular samples using information efficiently computed from the discriminator.

The authors use this diagnostic in three places. Example reweighting changes the influence of training examples, rejection sampling changes which generated outputs are retained, and active learning changes which data are selected. These applications respectively target training, inference, and data acquisition.

Across different image datasets, all three applications outperform their corresponding baselines. The abstract does not report the size of the gains or specify the exact estimation conditions behind the density-gap measure. The main contribution is a shared discriminator-based diagnostic that can guide several distinct stages of a conditional generation pipeline, rather than a wholly new generator architecture.

neurips-2019-mixtape-breaking-the-softma.tldr: Mixtape addresses the softmax bottleneck with much lower overhead than Mixture of Softmaxes.
paragraphs: A standard softmax output layer can limit the expressiveness of neural language models. Mixture of Softmaxes addresses that bottleneck but increases memory and computational costs. This paper introduces Mixtape, an alternative output layer designed to retain the expressive benefit with less overhead.

Mixtape combines logit-space vector gating, sigmoid-tree decomposition, and gate sharing. The authors evaluate it on four benchmarks spanning language modeling and machine translation, comparing both predictive quality and efficiency with Mixture of Softmaxes and ordinary softmax output layers.

The reported efficiency improvement over Mixture of Softmaxes ranges from 3.5x to 10.5x at similar performance. For vocabularies of 10–30K, a Mixtape-equipped network is 20% to 34% slower than a softmax-based network while improving perplexity and translation quality. These figures describe the tested configurations, illustrating a practical tradeoff between output-layer expressiveness and its computational cost.

neurips-2019-model-compression-with-adve.tldr: ATMC jointly optimizes compression, predictive accuracy, and adversarial robustness.
paragraphs: Model compression can preserve ordinary accuracy while changing a network’s behavior under adversarial attacks. This paper asks whether compact models can retain robustness as well as predictive performance, treating the three objectives together rather than assessing compression only through model size and standard accuracy.

The proposed Adversarially Trained Model Compression framework, ATMC, expresses the task as constrained optimization. Pruning, factorization, and quantization are integrated into the constraints, and the authors develop an efficient algorithm for solving the resulting formulation.

An extensive set of experiments reports more favorable tradeoffs among model size, accuracy, and robustness than available alternatives across multiple settings. The abstract does not list attack configurations, compression ratios, or numerical accuracies, so the robustness claim remains tied to those evaluated comparisons. The contribution is a unified optimization framework for balancing these competing requirements, not a guarantee of immunity to adversarial inputs.

neurips-2019-modelling-heterogeneous-dis.tldr: UMAL models complex regression uncertainty with an effectively infinite mixture and finitely many parameters.
paragraphs: Regression outputs may have skewed, multimodal, or otherwise complex distributions. Common parametric uncertainty models impose restrictive shapes that can miss those features. This paper introduces an Uncountable Mixture of Asymmetric Laplacians, or UMAL, to represent heterogeneous output distributions more flexibly.

The framework uses deep learning and connects its construction to quantile regression. Although it has a fixed number of parameters, it can be interpreted as an infinite mixture of components. This provides a way to model richer aleatoric uncertainty without explicitly assigning a separate parameter set to infinitely many components.

The authors evaluate synthetic cases, room-price forecasting, and prediction of financial operations in personal bank accounts. They report proper predictive distributions that support richer interpretation and decisions. The abstract gives no numerical comparison, calibration measure, or decision-outcome result, so it establishes the modeling approach and demonstrated applications rather than a quantified improvement in downstream decisions.

neurips-2019-non-asymptotic-analysis-of-.tldr: Stochastic proximal-gradient methods gain finite-time guarantees with nonconvex, nonsmooth regularizers.
paragraphs: Stochastic proximal-gradient methods are widely used when an objective includes a simple regularizer. Existing finite-time analyses for nonsmooth nonconvex problems generally required that regularizer itself to be convex. This paper addresses a smooth nonconvex loss combined with a regularizer that can be both nonsmooth and nonconvex.

The authors analyze several minibatch stochastic proximal-gradient variants. Their complexity for reaching an approximate stationary point matches the corresponding methods for convex-regularized nonconvex problems. They also develop variants that adjust minibatch sizes dynamically without requiring a target solution accuracy in advance.

Experiments compare the methods with other stochastic approaches and demonstrate their effectiveness. The theoretical target is approximate stationarity, not finding a global optimum of an arbitrary nonconvex objective. The abstract provides no particular complexity formulas or numerical results, but identifies both an expanded analysis regime and a practical adaptation that reduces dependence on advance tuning.

neurips-2019-objectnet-a-large-scale-bia.tldr: ObjectNet tests object recognition with controlled backgrounds, rotations, and viewpoints.
paragraphs: Image-recognition benchmarks can reward incidental correlations that do not transfer to new situations. ObjectNet addresses this by collecting images with randomized backgrounds, object rotations, and imaging viewpoints. Its objects are largely centered and unoccluded, making the challenge specifically about controlled variation rather than simply hiding the object.

The dataset contains 50,000 images, matching the size of the ImageNet test set, and deliberately has no paired training set. The authors build an automated crowdsourcing platform for controlled image capture and annotation, aiming to make this style of evaluation scalable.

Tested object detectors experience a reported 40–45% performance drop relative to other benchmarks, and fine-tuning produces only small gains. The abstract does not specify the absolute scores behind that drop. The contribution is both a diagnostic test set and a collection methodology designed to reveal reliance on dataset biases and encourage more transferable recognition.

neurips-2019-policy-learning-for-fairnes.tldr: Fair-PG-Rank learns stochastic rankings that balance user utility with fairness of item exposure.
paragraphs: Ranking systems affect both the users who consume results and the items or people being ranked. Conventional learning-to-rank optimizes user utility while often ignoring how visibility is distributed. This paper introduces a framework that combines utility objectives with fairness constraints on item exposure.

The framework allows stochastic ranking policies, providing a way to express fairness requirements over the rankings a system produces. Its Fair-PG-Rank algorithm uses policy gradients to search directly for fair ranking policies while supporting utility measures such as NDCG.

Theoretical development is accompanied by experiments on simulated and real-world datasets covering individual and group fairness. The results support the effectiveness of the approach in those settings. The abstract does not specify numerical utility costs or the exact fairness definitions used in each experiment, so fairness should be understood as satisfying the chosen exposure constraints rather than resolving every possible concern about a ranking system.

neurips-2019-reverse-kl-divergence-train.tldr: Reverse-KL training improves Prior Networks and increases the effort needed for evaluated adaptive attacks.
paragraphs: Prior Networks represent uncertainty by parameterizing a Dirichlet distribution over class-prediction distributions. Their original training objectives make scaling to many-class datasets difficult. This paper proposes reverse KL divergence between Dirichlet distributions as a training criterion that addresses problems with the target distributions.

The new objective supports classification with arbitrarily many classes and improves out-of-distribution detection. The authors then use it to investigate adversarial-attack detection and develop a generalized adversarial-training approach for Prior Networks.

On CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, successful adaptive white-box attacks that both change a prediction and evade detection require more computational effort than attacks against networks using standard adversarial training or MC-dropout. This is a comparative attack-effort result under the evaluated setup, not proof that attacks are impossible. The abstract does not state numerical attack budgets or certify a universal robustness bound.

neurips-2019-seeing-the-wind-visual-wind.tldr: Video of wind-driven motion can estimate local wind speed using coupled convolutional and recurrent networks.
paragraphs: Trees and flags visibly move in response to wind, potentially providing inexpensive measurements without dedicated sensors at every location. This paper investigates extracting wind speed from videos of those flow-structure interactions using a coupled convolutional and recurrent neural-network architecture.

The model is evaluated on naturally occurring wind affecting a flag and a tree. For speeds from 0.75 to 11 m/s, predictions agree with a cup anemometer on site, with root-mean-squared error approaching the natural variability caused by atmospheric turbulence.

Tests on other flags in the field and in a controlled wind tunnel demonstrate generalization beyond the original recordings. Physics-based scaling of flapping dynamics also predicts how frame rate and recording duration affect performance. The abstract does not claim universal transfer across every object or weather condition; it supports visual wind estimation for the tested structures and measurement ranges.

neurips-2019-smoothing-structured-decomp.tldr: Near-linear smoothing and linear-time all-marginals computation improve structured probabilistic circuits.
paragraphs: Probabilistic inference and density-estimation algorithms often require smooth circuits: every child of a plus gate must mention the same variables. Although this property is operationally important, the paper notes that the previously available general smoothing procedure was a straightforward quadratic-time algorithm.

The authors study smoothing as an algorithmic problem for structured decomposable circuits and propose a near-linear-time solution. They also examine lower bounds for smoothing decomposable circuits by connecting the task with existing results about range-sum queries.

For the important all-marginals case, they obtain a more efficient linear-time algorithm. Experiments validate the performance of the proposed methods. The different claims apply to different tasks and circuit assumptions; the abstract does not say that every arbitrary circuit can be smoothed in linear time. Its contribution is a sharper understanding of this preprocessing requirement together with faster algorithms in the specified settings.

neurips-2019-submodular-function-minimiz.tldr: Noisy submodular minimization has explicit error bounds, with optimal rates under multipoint feedback.
paragraphs: The paper studies minimizing a submodular function when evaluations contain zero-mean additive noise. Instead of assuming exact access to the objective, it asks how solution quality improves with the number of oracle calls T and the problem size n.

For ordinary feedback, the proposed algorithm achieves expected additive error O(n^(3/2)/sqrt(T)). A worst-case lower bound of Omega(n/sqrt(T)) limits how much that dependence can improve. These bounds describe optimization error from noisy information rather than exact recovery of the minimum.

The authors also allow each oracle call to return k function values. If every noisy oracle is itself submodular and 2 <= k = O(1), an algorithm achieves O(n/sqrt(T)) error with a matching lower bound up to constants. The optimality claim therefore belongs to this stronger feedback model and its additional assumptions, not automatically to the original single-value setting.

neurips-2020-a-self-tuning-actor-critic-.tldr: STAC adapts actor-critic hyperparameters online and improves scores across several reinforcement-learning benchmarks.
paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning performance often depends on manually tuned hyperparameters. Self-Tuning Actor-Critic, or STAC, uses metagradients to adapt differentiable actor-critic loss hyperparameters during learning. It also discovers auxiliary tasks and introduces a leaky V-trace operator for off-policy learning.

Ablations show performance improving as more hyperparameters are adapted. In the Arcade Learning Environment, median human-normalized score rises from 243% to 364% at 200M steps. In DM Control at 30M steps, mean score increases from 217 to 389 with features and from 108 to 202 with pixel inputs.

The Real-World Reinforcement Learning Challenge score increases from 195 to 295. The authors describe the method as sample efficient and requiring no significant compute increase. These are benchmark-specific outcomes under the reported training budgets, supporting online adaptation without establishing that manual tuning can be eliminated for every reinforcement-learning problem.

neurips-2020-adaptive-shrinkage-estimati.tldr: Adaptive sampling and shrinkage improve estimates of higher-order structure in streaming networks.
paragraphs: Large dynamic networks may arrive one edge at a time, making full storage and analysis infeasible. The paper focuses on estimating higher-order structural dependencies from small samples of such streams, rather than requiring observation of the complete network.

The authors propose a single-pass adaptive sampling framework with unbiased estimators for higher-order network analysis. The sampling method identifies edges that are especially informative for the structures being estimated. They also introduce a James–Stein shrinkage estimator to reduce estimation error.

The approach is analytic, computationally efficient, and supports incremental updates as the stream grows. Experiments on large networks show improvements over baseline methods. The abstract distinguishes the unbiased estimators from the additional shrinkage construction and does not state that every estimator retains unbiasedness. It also provides no numerical gains or exact memory requirements, so the empirical advantage remains tied to the reported comparisons.
